newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ashanti cuts Obuasi gold output target.
newsitem.headline: Ashanti cuts Obuasi gold output target.

text.p: Ashanti Goldfields Ltd said on Wednesday it had lowered its initial gold output targets from its flagship Obuasi mine in Ghana to 850,000 ounces a year from one million announced previously.
Trevor Schultz, Ashanti's chief operating officer told the Investment in African Mining Conference, that the group felt that the one million ounce forecast was not sustainable
"We feel that 850,000 ounces a year represents a very balanced level of production for the mine and we can produce quality ounces at that level of production," Schultz said.
The group, which has three operating mines in Ghana and one in Zimbabwe as well as two projects at an advanced stage of development, currently produces 1.1 million ounces of gold per year, he said.
"When we bring in the two new projects over the next 1 -1/2 to two years that will take our critical ounces up to 1.4 million a year," Schultz said.
Ashanti, which is 33.6 percent owned by British conglomerate Lonrho Plc, is also active in 25 exploration projects in 12 African countries.

Schultz said Obuasi was undergoing a fundamental transformation as surface operations, which have produced more than 50 percent of output for the past six years, were declining to be replaced by greater underground production.
"We will be nearly doubling the underground output from 1.9-2.0 million tonnes a year...to over 3.5 million tonnes over the next four years," he said.
Obuasi was expected to maintain a grade of over eight grammes per tonne with significant exploration potential present in especially the south side of the mine.
Schultz said the transformation of the mine -- a new shaft system would commence operation in March 1998 -- had come about through considerable capital expenditure.
"In 1996 we invested $147 million, this year a little over $110 million and next year $100-$110 million," he said, adding that expenditure would drop off considerably after that.
Rationalisation and cost-cutting exercises were in place which would see production costs stabilising at about $270 an ounce falling to $250 in 1998, he said.
